title: Luba: power and memory
question: How do institutions and memories sustain a political formation?
standfirst: Luba power can be read through institutions, insignia and practices that transmit history. An origin narrative and a royal object offer different kinds of evidence.

thesis.heading: An established presence, a debated origin

figures.claim: Luba state systems are established by this period at the latest.
figures.provenance: A latest bound used by Giacomo Macola, not a foundation year.

chapters.title: Governing and forming alliances
chapters.question: How does power extend beyond one court?
chapters.standfirst: Kingship alone does not describe every institution.

body.text: Bortolot describes sacred kingship alongside government by council. Alliances and the incorporation of neighbouring leaders help extend this political organisation.
The lupona at the Met expresses legitimacy connected to royal ancestors. Despite its shape, it is sacred insignia rather than ordinary furniture.

readings.label: A royal symbol
readings.body: Female figures on some seats refer to the spiritual role attributed to women in legitimising power.

readings.label: The object has its own date
readings.body: This lupona dates from the late nineteenth or early twentieth century. It is not a contemporary image of the earliest political formations.

illustration.alt: Carved seat supported by a female figure decorated with beads.
illustration.caption: Luba lupona, late nineteenth–early twentieth century. An insignia of power preserved in a museum.

chapters.title: Transmitting history
chapters.question: How is political history preserved?
chapters.standfirst: Material supports accompany practices of memory.

body.text: Lukasa are memory aids. The Smithsonian associates them with royal histories, king lists and significant events: their function extends beyond decoration.
The Genesis catalogue describes beads and signs interpreted through people, places and relationships. Reading them requires knowledge; a photograph alone does not deliver the narrative.

readings.label: Organised memory
readings.body: The lukasa connects history to a handheld support. It invites us to consider oral transmission as a practice of knowledge.

readings.label: A chronology to refine
readings.body: Macola places imperial expansion in the eighteenth century and describes destabilised Luba and Lunda networks in the late nineteenth. These stages do not date a legendary founder.

gaps.reason: The narratives of Kalala Ilunga do not establish a single foundation date here. This dossier does not describe every population bearing a Luba name today.
